It also improves the performance of artificial intelligence systems, fostering trust and adoption while generating value. We help companies develop and operationalize a custom-fit framework for responsible AI. Emerging regulations and generative AI are casting a spotlight on AI technology, but they don’t need to cast a shadow. Our perspective is that responsible AI is more than just risk mitigation, as it also an important value creator. What’s the holdup? For some organizations, the leap from responsible AI ambition to execution has proved daunting. Others are waiting to see what form regulations take. But responsible AI principles can bring benefits now as they prepare companies for new rules and the latest emerging AI technology. Our battle-tested BCG RAI framework minimizes the time to RAI maturity while maximizing the value responsible AI can create. Firm-specific AI offerings and product/service portfolios

The major consulting firms in this set differ in how clearly they position AI as a product portfolio versus as a broader transformation capability. McKinsey is notable for framing AI through its case-study-rich “Tech and AI” page, which highlights how it partners with clients to rewire organizations and outcompete with technology, and explicitly includes generative AI (Lilli) as a major product line [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Its AI offerings are strongly client-facing and mission-aligned with organizational transformation, including claims of faster claims settlement, decarbonization planning, cybersecurity purchasing platforms, and AI-driven carbon and digital transformation projects [N1-F1]. BCG and McKinsey also overlap in emphasizing strategic AI transformation, with BCG’s “AI @ Scale” page describing execution of a comprehensive AI business transformation and its responsible AI program as a tailored strategic approach [N3-R3][N3-R2][N3-F3]. McKinsey’s evidence shows it uses AI across cost transformation, digital transformation, and industry-specific projects such as insurance, energy, and banking, while BCG emphasizes strategic AI and responsible AI as core pillars of its offering [N1-R2][N3-R2][N3-F3].

Accenture presents AI as a broader “Data and Advanced AI” portfolio, with a case-study page listing generative AI, cloud, software engineering, and industry-specific solutions [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Its evidence also shows a clear emphasis on customer experience, business reinvention, and transformation stories, including AI-powered virtual assistants, personalized recommendations, and GenAI in banking and retail [N2-F2]. Accenture’s case studies are particularly broad in functional use cases, covering customer experience, business reinvention, and AI-powered virtual assistance, which suggests a more client-facing product mindset than McKinsey’s more transformational framing [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence is the most explicit about modular AI services: its services page describes a “Resonance AI Framework” and “RAISE™” as enterprise AI foundations, while also listing AI-powered experiences, go-to-market solutions, business process operations, and IT services [N4-F4]. Capgemini’s offerings are highly modular and enterprise-ready, with a clear emphasis on AI foundations, scalable AI, and business-process augmentation [N4-F4].

McKinsey, BCG, and Accenture all have strong evidence for client-facing AI applications, but McKinsey’s page is the most explicitly case-study-heavy, with examples spanning insurance, energy, banking, and sustainability [N1-F1]. Accenture’s evidence is similarly rich in case studies but leans more toward customer experience, transformation, and business reinvention [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence shows a broader product-service stack, including AI foundations, experiences, go-to-market, process operations, and IT services, indicating a wider product breadth than the other firms’ evidence suggests [N4-F4]. BCG’s evidence is stronger on strategic AI and responsible AI than on specific client products, with a clear emphasis on a tailored five-pillar RAI program and enterprise AI enablement [N3-R2][N3-F3].

Specialization differences are evident: McKinsey is strongest in transformational AI use cases across industry, including decarbonization, cybersecurity, and digital banking [N1-F1]; Accenture is strongest in customer experience, transformation, and business reinvention with AI [N2-F2]; Capgemini is strongest in modular enterprise AI architecture, AI foundations, and cross-functional AI capabilities such as IT, marketing, and operations [N4-F4]; and BCG is strongest in strategic AI execution and responsible AI governance [N3-R2][N3-F3]. The evidence also suggests a clear difference in framing: McKinsey and BCG emphasize organizational and strategic transformation, Accenture emphasizes business reinvention and customer-facing AI, and Capgemini emphasizes scalable AI infrastructure and modular product architecture [N1-F1][N3-R2][N4-F4].

Client case studies and application scenarios

The evidence points to a broad range of industry and functional use cases across the firms. McKinsey’s case studies include insurance claims processing, banking digital transformation, aluminum operations, telecom employee training, decarbonization planning, cybersecurity purchasing platforms, and AI-driven talent development [N1-F1]. Accenture’s case studies include customer experience, business reinvention, and AI-powered virtual assistants, with specific examples such as Best Buy, BBVA, Bricorama, and Noli in retail, banking, and consumer products [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence describes AI-powered experiences, go-to-market, business process operations, and IT services, with examples in customer-facing AI, personalized recommendations, and industrial operations such as manufacturing and supply chains [N4-F4]. BCG’s evidence is thinner on specific client case studies, but it does indicate AI use in business transformation, cost transformation, and responsible AI governance [N3-R2][N3-R3].

The most representative industry use cases are banking, insurance, manufacturing, retail, energy, and telecommunications. In banking, McKinsey worked with Emirates NBD on AI and advanced analytics, and with Deutsche Telekom on AI-powered training and coaching tools [N1-F1]. In insurance, McKinsey helped Aviva rewire the claims journey with AI, improving speed, accuracy, and outcomes [N1-F1]. In manufacturing, McKinsey supported Emirates Global Aluminium and MEXT, while Accenture’s Bricorama case shows AI helping a DIY retailer provide expert advice on painting projects [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In retail, Accenture’s Best Buy case shows generative AI used to enhance customer and employee experiences [N2-F2]. In energy, McKinsey worked with Xcel Energy and Formula E, and Capgemini’s evidence includes AI in energy-sector transformation and digital capabilities [N1-F1][N4-F4].

Common functional use cases across firms include customer service automation, claims processing, talent development, cybersecurity, and supply chain optimization. McKinsey’s Aviva case shows AI improving claims settlement [N1-F1], while Accenture’s case studies show AI used in customer experience, virtual assistants, and sales/marketing automation [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence points to AI in customer-facing operations, manufacturing, and IT, including self-optimizing systems, logistics, and code engineering [N4-F4]. BCG’s responsible AI framework is more functional as governance than as a client-use case, but it still implies AI implementation across business functions through responsible AI governance, product development, and continuous improvement [N3-F3].

What each case achieved or claimed to achieve is generally summarized in the evidence as faster outcomes, better customer experience, higher efficiency, and measurable value. McKinsey claims AI helped Aviva settle claims faster and more accurately [N1-F1], Emirates NBD expand talent and become AI-driven [N1-F1], and Xcel Energy improve spend and carbon transparency [N1-F1]. Accenture claims AI enhanced Best Buy’s customer and employee experiences, improved sales and marketing through personalized recommendations, and helped BBVA become more customer-centric [N2-F2]. Capgemini claims AI can improve customer experiences, augment service and marketing operations, and enable self-optimizing industrial systems [N4-F4]. BCG’s evidence suggests responsible AI can improve performance, foster trust, and create value through guardrails and innovation [N3-F3].

The pain points addressed by AI solutions are broadly automation, inefficiency, and risk. McKinsey’s evidence points to AI transforming operations, optimizing cost programs, and enabling decarbonization planning [N1-F1]. Accenture’s evidence points to improving customer experience, personalization, and efficiency [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence points to better process performance, reduced manual effort, and improved decision-making in industrial and IT operations [N4-F4]. BCG’s evidence explicitly ties AI to risk, governance, and the need to address third-party AI risks [N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that AI consulting is being positioned to solve operational bottlenecks, improve customer and employee experience, and manage AI-related risk through governance and implementation [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

The evidence indicates that major consulting firms are positioning AI as a strategic and operational transformation tool rather than merely a technical product. McKinsey’s “Tech and AI” case-study page shows AI being used to rewire organizations and outcompete with technology, while its 2025 AI report and case studies emphasize digital, operational, and skills transformation [N1-R1][N1-F1]. BCG’s “AI @ Scale” page and responsible AI page show AI as a strategic opportunity for comprehensive business transformation and as a governance challenge requiring a tailored five-pillar RAI program [N3-R3][N3-R2][N3-F3]. Accenture’s evidence also frames AI around business reinvention and transformation, with a clear emphasis on AI-driven transformation and responsible AI governance [N2-R5][N3-F3]. Capgemini’s evidence shows AI as a transformational architecture, with a Resonance AI Framework and RAISE™ designed to scale AI and accelerate adoption [N4-F4]. This common pattern across firms suggests that AI is being treated as a strategic transformation lever, not just an incremental improvement.

Emerging trends such as generative AI, ethics, and explainability are central to the evidence. BCG explicitly frames responsible AI as a strategic issue involving fairness, accountability, transparency, and compliance, with ARTKIT as a toolkit for testing GenAI systems for proficiency, safety, equality, security, and compliance [N3-F3]. Accenture’s case studies and the broader consulting evidence also point to generative AI in customer experience, business reinvention, and transformation [N2-F2]. Explainability is not explicitly named, but responsible AI governance and testing mechanisms imply a strong emphasis on transparency and trustworthy AI [N3-F3].

Firms are positioning AI as a strategic or operational transformation tool in three ways. First, they are using AI to reshape business functions and processes at scale. McKinsey’s evidence shows AI used to optimize cost transformation, decarbonize supply chains, and transform operations [N1-F1]. BCG’s evidence shows AI strategy consulting and responsible AI as parts of a comprehensive transformation approach [N3-R3][N3-F3]. Capgemini’s evidence frames AI as a transformational architecture and a way to accelerate value creation through AI foundations and modular AI assets [N4-F4]. Third, they are linking AI to business performance and measurable outcomes. McKinsey’s evidence claims faster claims processing and better outcomes; Accenture’s evidence claims improved customer and employee experiences; Capgemini’s evidence claims better process performance and business value [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

The evidence also suggests that the future priorities are increasingly about AI at scale, responsible AI, and generative AI adoption. BCG’s “AI @ Scale” page emphasizes a 10-20-70 approach, though the exact breakdown is incomplete in the provided evidence [N7-R3]. BCG’s responsible AI evidence shows a clear future focus on guardrails, culture, and continuous improvement [N3-F3]. Accenture’s evidence points to generative AI as a central theme across multiple transformation areas [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence emphasizes AI foundations, modular assets, and AI-powered IT [N4-F4]. McKinsey’s evidence reinforces AI as a strategic transformation lever across multiple industries [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a strategic direction in which AI is being positioned as a transformational enabler, with a strong emphasis on governance, generative AI, and responsible AI implementation [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R1].

# Integrated global summary of AI investments, key initiatives, and outputs by major consulting firms

The evidence provided shows a broad but uneven picture of how major consulting firms are organizing their AI work. McKinsey, BCG, Accenture, and Capgemini are the strongest sources in this set, with McKinsey especially rich in case studies and transformational framing, BCG especially strong on strategic and governance-led AI, Accenture especially broad in customer-facing AI and transformation stories, and Capgemini especially focused on modular enterprise AI and product architecture. The evidence also shows that consulting firms are increasingly positioning AI not just as a technical product or service, but as a strategic transformation lever, with strong emphasis on governance, responsible AI, and operational transformation [N1-F1][N3-R3][N3-R2][N3-F3][N2-F2][N4-F4].

## 1) Firm-specific AI offerings and product/service portfolios

### McKinsey
McKinsey’s evidence positions AI as a transformational capability rather than a narrow product line. Its case-study page shows AI used across multiple industries and functions, including insurance claims processing, banking digital transformation, aluminum operations, telecom employee training, decarbonization planning, cybersecurity purchasing platforms, and AI-driven talent development [N1-F1]. McKinsey’s evidence also explicitly mentions generative AI (Lilli) as part of its AI portfolio, and it frames AI as a tool to rewire organizations and outcompete with technology [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This suggests a broad client-facing product/service orientation centered on organizational transformation, digital transformation, and industry-specific AI applications.

### BCG
BCG’s evidence is stronger on strategic AI execution than on specific client products. It describes AI strategy consulting and responsible AI as core capabilities, with a tailored five-pillar RAI program and a battle-tested AI implementation framework [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F3]. BCG’s emphasis on responsible AI governance, AI governance, continuous improvement, and internal AI enablement indicates a more governance-and-strategy-focused product portfolio than McKinsey’s transformational case-study orientation [N3-F3]. BCG also emphasizes AI as part of business transformation and as a strategic opportunity for scale, which implies a broader consulting-service orientation than a product line [N3-R3].

### Accenture
Accenture’s evidence is strong on case studies and transformational AI applications. Its “Data and Advanced AI” page and client stories indicate generative AI, cloud, software engineering, and industry-specific solutions, with a clear emphasis on customer experience, business reinvention, and transformation [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Accenture’s evidence also includes AI-powered virtual assistants, personalized recommendations, and AI-enabled banking, showing a broad client-facing product stack focused on business transformation and operational improvement [N2-F2]. This makes Accenture’s offering more product-like and transformation-oriented than BCG’s governance-focused model.

### Capgemini
Capgemini’s evidence is the most explicitly productized. Its services page describes a “Resonance AI Framework,” RAISE™, and a modular enterprise AI architecture, while also listing AI-powered experiences, go-to-market solutions, business process operations, and IT services [N4-F4]. This suggests a more infrastructure- and modular-product focused offering, with AI embedded in customer-facing, operational, and IT capabilities. Capgemini’s framing emphasizes scalability, adoption, and enterprise AI foundations, which makes its portfolio more about enabling AI across business functions than about specific client case studies [N4-F4].

### Differences in specialization across firms
The firms’ specializations are distinct. McKinsey specializes in transformational AI across industries, with a strong case-study portfolio [N1-F1]. BCG specializes in strategic AI execution and responsible AI governance [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F3]. Accenture specializes in customer experience, business reinvention, and transformation with AI [N2-F2]. Capgemini specializes in modular enterprise AI architecture and AI-enabled business-process operations [N4-F4]. The evidence also suggests a clear difference in framing: McKinsey and BCG are more transformation and governance oriented, while Accenture and Capgemini are more product and implementation oriented [N1-R1][N3-F3][N2-F2][N4-F4].

## 2) Client case studies and application scenarios

### Industry and functional use cases
The evidence spans several industries and functions:

- **Banking:** McKinsey worked with Emirates NBD and Deutsche Telekom on AI and advanced analytics; Accenture’s BBVA case shows AI in customer-centric banking [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Insurance:** McKinsey helped Aviva rewire the claims journey with AI, improving speed, accuracy, and outcomes [N1-F1].
- **Manufacturing:** McKinsey supported Emirates Global Aluminium and MEXT; Accenture’s Bricorama case shows AI helping a DIY retailer provide expert advice on painting projects [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Retail:** Accenture’s Best Buy case shows generative AI enhancing customer and employee experiences [N2-F2].
- **Energy and sustainability:** McKinsey worked with Xcel Energy and Formula E; Capgemini’s evidence includes AI in energy-sector transformation and digital capabilities [N1-F1][N4-F4].
- **Telecom and HR:** McKinsey’s evidence includes AI for telecom employee training and talent development; IBM’s evidence shows AI in HR and talent processes such as recruiting, retaining, and developing skills [N1-F1][N4-R1].

### What each case achieved or claimed to achieve
The evidence consistently highlights faster outcomes, better customer experience, higher efficiency, and measurable value. McKinsey claims faster claims settlement, AI-driven transformation, and better operational outcomes [N1-F1]. Accenture claims improved customer and employee experiences, better sales and marketing through personalized recommendations, and more customer-centric banking [N2-F2]. Capgemini claims improved customer experiences, better process performance, and business value through AI-powered operations and IT [N4-F4]. BCG’s evidence is more indirect on specific outcomes, but it emphasizes responsible AI as a value-creation framework that can improve performance, foster trust, and reduce risk [N3-F3].

### Common pain points addressed
The common pain points across the evidence are automation bottlenecks, inefficiency, risk management, and transformation complexity. McKinsey’s evidence points to AI transforming operations, optimizing cost programs, and enabling decarbonization planning [N1-F1]. Accenture’s evidence points to improving customer experience and business transformation [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence points to better process performance and enterprise AI adoption [N4-F4]. BCG’s evidence explicitly ties AI to risk, governance, and third-party AI risks, showing that AI implementation is often framed as a governance problem as much as a technical one [N3-F3].

## 3) Strategic directions and future priorities

### Firms’ stated AI roadmaps and priorities
The evidence shows that firms are increasingly framing AI as a strategic transformation agenda, not merely a technical capability. McKinsey’s evidence emphasizes digital, operational, and skills transformation [N1-R1][N1-F1]. BCG emphasizes AI @ Scale and responsible AI as strategic priorities, with a 10-20-70 implementation approach and a five-pillar RAI framework [N3-R3][N3-R2][N3-F3]. Accenture frames AI around business reinvention and transformation [N2-F2]. Capgemini emphasizes AI foundations, modular assets, and enterprise AI scaling [N4-F4]. This indicates that firms are aligning AI with broader business transformation rather than as a standalone product.

### Emerging trends
Several emerging trends are central to the evidence:

- **Generative AI:** BCG explicitly discusses generative AI in responsible AI and ARTKIT, while Accenture’s evidence shows generative AI in customer experience and business transformation [N3-F3][N2-F2].
- **Ethics and responsible AI:** This is the most prominent trend. BCG’s evidence is especially detailed on responsible AI, governance, and compliance, with ARTKIT as a tool for testing GenAI systems for safety, fairness, security, and compliance [N3-F3]. The evidence also includes broader AI ethics themes, such as fairness, accountability, transparency, and privacy [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].
- **Explainability and governance:** While not explicitly named, responsible AI governance and testing mechanisms imply a strong emphasis on explainability and trustworthy AI [N3-F3].

### Positioning AI as a strategic or operational transformation tool
The firms position AI as both a strategic and operational tool. McKinsey positions AI as a way to outcompete with technology and rewire organizations [N1-R1][N1-F1]. BCG positions AI as a strategic transformation lever and responsible AI as part of a broader governance architecture [N3-R3][N3-F3]. Accenture positions AI as part of business reinvention and transformation [N2-F2]. Capgemini positions AI as an enterprise AI architecture and transformation tool [N4-F4]. The evidence also suggests that AI is being embedded into business processes, customer-facing operations, and internal IT, which strengthens the case for AI as a transformation driver rather than a standalone product [N4-F4].

## 4) Talent development and workforce programs

### Upskilling, reskilling, and certification programs
The evidence is thinner on formal certification programs than on workforce transformation, but the broader context is clear. IBM’s evidence shows AI expanding across HR processes such as recruiting, retaining, and developing talent [N4-R1]. Accenture’s evidence suggests AI is used to improve customer and employee experience, implying reskilling and upskilling in service and transformation work [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence indicates AI is part of talent development and talent strategy, with a focus on AI-powered IT and business-process augmentation [N4-F4]. BCG’s evidence emphasizes continuous improvement and internal governance, which supports ongoing workforce development through responsible AI [N3-F3].

### Internal AI talent pipelines and development pathways
The evidence does not provide a detailed internal AI talent pipeline for each firm, but it does show internal development pathways. BCG’s responsible AI framework includes a responsible AI council, continuous improvement processes, and internal governance structures, which suggest a structured internal pathway for AI talent [N3-F3]. Capgemini’s Resonance AI Framework and RAISE™ indicate a modular internal development approach for AI implementation and enterprise scaling [N4-F4]. Accenture’s case studies and business reinvention evidence imply a workforce-development orientation, though the evidence is less explicit about internal pipelines [N2-F2].

### How firms attract and retain AI expertise
The evidence suggests that firms attract and retain AI expertise through governance, partnership, and internal enablement. BCG uses a responsible AI council and continuous improvement to retain expertise and foster ownership [N3-F3]. Capgemini uses a modular enterprise AI architecture and RAISE™ to retain and scale AI capabilities [N4-F4]. Accenture’s transformation-oriented case studies imply attraction through client-facing AI delivery, while IBM’s talent-development evidence suggests retention through HR-enabled AI augmentation [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Overall, the evidence points to a mix of governance, partnership, and internal enablement as the main mechanisms for attracting and retaining AI expertise [N3-F3][N4-F4][N4-R2].

## 5) Cross-firm comparisons and distinct analytical subproblems

### Differences between Big Four versus MBB versus other firms
The evidence supports a partial comparison. McKinsey is the most evidence-rich in this set, with a large case-study portfolio and broad industry examples [N1-F1]. BCG is the clearest example of MBB-style consulting, with a strong emphasis on strategic AI and responsible AI [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F3]. Accenture and Capgemini are better represented as “other major international consulting firms,” with Accenture emphasizing client-facing transformation and Capgemini emphasizing modular AI architecture [N2-F2][N4-F4]. The evidence does not fully cover all Big Four firms, so the comparison is partial and should be treated cautiously.

### How consulting firms report AI versus how they implement AI
The difference is clear in the evidence. McKinsey reports AI through client case studies and transformation claims [N1-F1]. BCG reports AI through strategic frameworks and responsible AI governance [N3-F3]. Accenture reports AI through case studies and transformation stories [N2-F2]. Capgemini reports AI through product architecture and modular services [N4-F4]. This suggests that BCG and McKinsey are stronger on strategic and governance reporting, while Accenture and Capgemini are stronger on implementation and productization.

### Gaps in evidence across firm types
The evidence has notable gaps. McKinsey’s evidence is the most comprehensive, with the largest case-study set [N1-F1]. BCG’s evidence is strong on strategy and governance but thinner on client-specific case studies [N3-R2][N3-F3]. Accenture’s evidence is strong on business reinvention and customer-facing AI, but it does not fully expose an internal implementation framework [N2-F2]. Capgemini’s evidence is strong on product architecture, but it is also more abstract than McKinsey’s [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a conclusion that Big Four and MBB firms are better represented in the provided sources, while evidence for other major consulting firms is thinner and less detailed.

## 6) Integrated conclusion

The global picture across major consulting firms is one of broad but distinct AI strategies:

- **McKinsey** leads in transformational AI with a strong case-study portfolio and a broad set of industry applications [N1-F1].
- **BCG** leads in strategic AI and responsible AI, with a clear governance and implementation framework [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F3].
- **Accenture** leads in client-facing AI, business reinvention, and transformation stories [N2-F2].
- **Capgemini** leads in modular enterprise AI architecture and AI-enabled business-process services [N4-F4].

The common themes are:
- AI as a **strategic transformation tool**, not just a technical product [N1-R1][N3-R3][N2-F2][N4-F4].
- Increasing emphasis on **generative AI, ethics, and responsible AI** [N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].
- A growing need for **internal governance, continuous improvement, and talent development** [N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2].
- A clear divide between **strategic/governance-led AI** and **product/implementation-led AI** [N3-R2][N2-F2][N4-F4].

The evidence also shows a gap in firm coverage, especially for non-MBB and non-McKinsey consulting firms. For a complete global picture, more detailed evidence would be needed for Deloitte, EY, and other major firms, but the provided material already supports a strong conclusion that consulting firms are converging on AI as a transformational capability while differentiating by strategic focus, governance, productization, and client-facing implementation [N1-F1][N3-F3][N2-F2][N4-F4].

The global picture across major consulting firms is one of broad but distinct AI strategies:
